questions.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2,$ and the lines $y=x+2,$ $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/019f0f9f83ddf323d543d109677335cb3ae72a200baf834453a0eca16a9353ba.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/d222e86f6af7c3ed2b35711114c9062d6f0c9b0f2551aa44cac33318c6e5813f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,x+2\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\le y\le x+2\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{x+2}^{{x}^{2}/2+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/2+2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le x\le -2,\,0\le y\le \frac{3x}{2}+6\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le -1,\,0\le y\le -3x-3\}.

questions.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=6-4x$ and $y=2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=\sqrt{x-2}+1,$ and the lines $y=2-\frac{1}{2}x$ and $y=8-2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=\sqrt{x-2}+1 & \,⟹\,x=(y-1)^{2}+2 \\ y=2-\frac{1}{2}x & \,⟹\,x=4-2y \\ y=8-2x & \,⟹\,x=4-\frac{1}{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/3f8e3ccfeac236d7fe9a502f599c61c404607a55ae809ec142019a3f881e1568.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/3148cb0f499564db9cbfd6b635fef81dc47298789241af4a243c32dbf4dc8247.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,4-2y\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,(y-1)^{2}+2\le x\le 4-\frac{1}{2}y\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{4-2y}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(y-1)^{2}+2}^{4-y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${∬}_{D}2y\,dA,$ where $D$ is the region shown in the picture above.
questions.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/33a38da74b282f0ec1fb2fae9cb155feb2a5fd39128c7607b80c6b84fedd29b4.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,x-1\le y\le 3-x\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,3-x\le y\le x-1\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{x-1}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{3-x}^{x-1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{x-1}^{3-x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{3-x}^{x-1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}[(x-1)^{2}-(3-x)^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-4x)\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}(4x-8)\text{d}x \\  & =(8x-2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{2}+(2{x}^{2}-8x){|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =8(2-1)-2({2}^{2}-{1}^{2})+2({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})-8(4-2) \\  & =8-6+24-16 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/2fcb30778db2f051a7a819ae701808af59ac18d27c25a9c57ce678caa6c3ee3b.png)

{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le -x\}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x\}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2x\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2x\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{-x}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2xy{|}_{{x}^{2}}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}2x[-x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}2x[x-{x}^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{-1}^{0}+{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =((0-(-\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{4}))+((\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{4})-0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type I Regions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y= 2^x,$ $y=\sqrt{x}$  and lines $x=0$ and $y=2,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of a function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/b80527fdef6f890581b8f56431e1b72a8f7eae3b41827caa16486ed9f2fd45ea.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/939e46b3ed4266f3c18d3567f951276e420292781cfc414711c244f453bc4029.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2^x \big\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x  \leq 4, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{{2}^{x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=2+\ln x,$  and the lines $y=1$, $x=1,$ and  $x=e,$  as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/4b0dff15fa9fa93ed61183702bff6bb443daf14b0adbf56cf4b97e3bd830ceea.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2+\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,x={e}^{y-2}\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/2228ad860fea1e2c30d20bce749f654da02a97c65fd5e70152a07761e26f3e78.png)

    

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y  \leq 2, \quad 1 \leq x \leq e \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 2 \leq y  \leq 3, \quad e^{y-2} \leq x \leq e\bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{{e}^{y-2}}^{e}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Partitioned Region
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/1d180fd5de88ebc465df522879142e5a4c5446c758aaccde792092968078c254.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed by the curves $x=2y^3-2y$ and  $x=y^3-4y,$ and the $y$-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/6812e8036df171e162bee49d2edcff6d4a742e7bb4f14247713bd2332c64ccc6.png)

 

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y  \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y  \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}-4y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-2{y}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0}+{[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral  

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $D$ is the finite region bounded by the lines $x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,$ and $y=x.$ How do we proceed?

To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps: 

**Step 1.** Sketch the region $D$. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral. 

In this example, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/0a90a4f377327f5293308f1e08ac6596f1c27b9bd47a614d6d7cb1c5dbfec33c.png)

**Step 2.** Split (if necessary) the region $D$ into several type I or II regions.

From the diagram above, we see that our region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as follows.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14153479/assets/a93e1a0a0a7f9c104cb5d380b2a7ff98d6712ef0d2d67b74130da5dcf1701443.png)

 

So, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}
$$

and

$$
D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2,  \quad  x \leq y \leq 3-x\}
$$

**Step 3.** Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

*If $D$ is the union of two sub-regions, $D_1, D_2$, that don't overlap then,*

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.
$$

So, finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}2(x+y)\text{ }dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{3/2}{\int }_{x}^{3-x}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
